summary: Describes an architecture for indexing distributed databases and applies it to the WHOIS++ directory protocol. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine many libraries each with their own catalog, plus a master list that tells you which library to ask. This described such a system for looking up people and things.

questions: how does the whois++ index service work
subtitle: Architecture for indexing a distributed network of directory servers.

tldr.problem: Hierarchical directory services like X.500 have search and naming problems: searches must be directed to the right location in a rigid namespace, and queries that don't match the namespace structure require expensive global searches that burden every server.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a directory mesh architecture where index servers collect centroids (summaries of word lists) from lower-level servers, allowing queries to be intelligently routed without global replication. Servers can participate in multiple hierarchies, and new special-purpose directories can be easily constructed by pooling servers.
tldr.outcome: The Whois++ protocol and Index Service architecture are now historic. Modern directory and search systems use different approaches, including distributed databases and search engines.

today: RFC 1913 describes the Whois++ Index Service architecture and is now Historic. The Whois++ protocol itself and related indexing systems have been superseded by more modern directory and search technologies. Today's directory services typically use different approaches, such as distributed databases, search engines, and web-based APIs, rather than the template-based query model used by Whois++.

sections.title: Introduction to Distributed Directory Services
sections.content:
The Whois++ directory service is an extensible directory system for finding people and information on the Internet. It uses a template-based information model and a flexible query language. However, building a single centralized directory for all Internet information is infeasible. A distributed approach is needed, where many Whois++ servers each hold their own information.

Earlier hierarchical approaches (like X.500) imposed a rigid namespace tree: every record had a fixed location, and searches that did not match the namespace structure required queries to be replicated globally to all servers. This is expensive and does not scale well. RFC 1913 defines a new architecture that solves these problems by creating a directory mesh with intelligent query routing.
sections.plainLanguage: Whois++ is a system for looking up people and places on the internet. With many servers spread out, we need a smart way to route questions to the right servers without asking everyone.

sections.title: Directory Meshes and Forward Knowledge
sections.content:
The key innovation is the directory mesh, a layer of index servers on top of the base servers. Each index server maintains forward knowledge about the contents of servers below it, allowing it to route queries intelligently. When a query arrives, the index server checks its forward knowledge, prunes the search tree, and forwards the query only to servers likely to have matching records.

Rather than a rigid tree hierarchy, the mesh topology allows flexibility: a base server can be indexed by multiple index servers, and index servers can themselves be indexed by higher-level index servers. This enables multiple hierarchies to coexist on the same data. The architecture decouples the entry identifier (unique location) from the navigation service, so searches are not bound by the namespace structure.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a simple tree where each library has one parent, we create a mesh where a library can have multiple parents. Each parent keeps track of what topics the child knows about, so queries get routed smartly.

sections.title: Centroids and Forward Knowledge
sections.content:
A centroid is a summary of a server's contents, comprising a list of templates and attributes the server holds, plus a word list for each attribute. The word list contains every unique word appearing at least once in that attribute across all records in the server. A word is any token delimited by spaces, newlines, or the '@' character.

For example, if a server has three user records with names John Smith, Joe Smith, and contacts named Mike and Foobar, the centroid would list the templates, attribute names, and words: 'John', 'Joe', 'Smith' under First Name and Last Name; 'Mike', 'Foobar' under Contact Name. This compact summary is handed up to index servers, allowing them to determine which servers might have records matching a query without querying the servers directly.
sections.plainLanguage: A centroid is a list of every unique word in a library's catalog. If someone asks 'do you have books about cooking?', the index checks its centroid word lists and can say 'yes, check Library A' or 'no, we don't have that word'.

sections.title: Index Server Architecture and Query Handling
sections.content:
An index server collects and maintains the centroids of either base Whois++ servers or other index servers. When a query arrives, the index server searches its collection of centroids to determine which lower-level servers hold records that might satisfy the query. It then sends a referral to the client, indicating which servers to contact next. An index server can also hold primary data itself, acting as both an index server and a base server.

Centroid propagation is initiated by an authenticated POLL command. The polled server responds with a CENTROID-CHANGES report, transmitting either the complete centroid or just changes since the last poll. The polling server can authenticate the response before incorporating it. This mechanism supports both periodic polling and reactive updates: a server can issue a DATA-CHANGED command to notify pollers that its centroid has changed, allowing them to update their information promptly.
sections.plainLanguage: Index servers regularly ask lower-level servers 'what words do you have?' and build a combined list. When a search comes in, the index looks at its list and tells the client which servers to ask.

sections.title: Mesh Topology, Loop Detection, and Replication
sections.content:
The mesh architecture allows flexible, multi-level indexing without a fixed tree structure. When an index server polls another server, it can indicate the relationship (topology, geographical, or administrative) to help with query routing. Each server maintains a hop count, defined as the maximum hop count of all servers it polls, plus one. Base-level servers have a hop count of zero. A maximum hop count (8 in the current version) helps detect polling loops, preventing infinite loops in the mesh.

The protocols are designed to support server replication for redundancy and robustness. Forward knowledge propagation works equally well for replication: instead of just centroid word lists, the complete database of a replicated server can be handed around. This allows multiple copies of a server's data to exist in the mesh, improving availability and load distribution across the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers can have multiple parents and can form meshes without creating loops. The system counts how many hops up from a base server you are; if that number gets too high, there's a loop. Servers can also be duplicated for safety.
